blocks.p: **Oh! {{-네요|-neyo}}.** Stem + {{-네요|-neyo}} reacts to something you've just noticed or found out: {{좋네요!|jonneyo!}} “Oh, it's nice!”, {{비싸네요|bissaneyo}} “Wow, it's expensive.” When you react, it sounds much more natural than the plain {{좋아요|joayo}}. For something already done: {{-았/었네요|-at/eonneyo}}, {{많이 했네요!|mani haenneyo!}} “You've done a lot!”. Stems ending in {{ㄹ}} drop it: {{멀다|meolda}} → {{머네요|meoneyo}}, {{불다|bulda}} → {{부네요|buneyo}}.

**Right? {{-죠?|-jyo?}}** Stem + {{-죠?|-jyo?}} (short for {{-지요?|-jiyo?}}) asks the other person to agree with something you both know or feel: {{춥죠?|chupjyo?}} “It's cold, isn't it?”, {{맛있죠?|masitjyo?}} “It's good, right?”. Said flat, it's a soft “of course”: {{그렇죠.|geureochyo.}} “That's right.” With a question word, it's a gentle question: {{이름이 뭐죠?|ireumi mwojyo?}} “What was your name again?”

**{{-군요|-gunyo}}.** In dramas, books and careful speech you'll hear {{-군요|-gunyo}} (after action verbs, {{-는군요|-neungunyo}}): {{그렇군요|geureokunyo}} “I see”, {{바쁘시군요|bappeusigunyo}} “you're busy, I see”. Like {{-네요|-neyo}}, it's for something you've just understood. Recognising it is enough.

blocks.p: **Describing comes first.** In English, what describes a noun can come after it: “the man **drinking coffee**”, “a friend **who lives in Busan**”. In Korean, everything that describes a noun comes **before** it, and the verb takes a modifier ending: {{커피를 마시는 사람|keopireul masineun saram}} “the person drinking coffee” (coffee drink-ing person).

blocks.means: an ending that turns a verb into a describing word placed before a noun: {{마시다|masida}} → {{마시는 사람|masineun saram}} “a person who drinks”, {{작다|jakda}} → {{작은 가방|jageun gabang}} “a small bag”.

blocks.p: **Two endings for now.** Action verbs, and words with {{있다|itda}}/{{없다|eopda}}, take {{-는|-neun}}: {{마시는|masineun}}, {{먹는|meongneun}}, {{맛있는|masinneun}}. Descriptive verbs take {{-ㄴ}} after a vowel and {{-은|-eun}} after a consonant: {{예쁜|yeppeun}}, {{작은|jageun}}. Stems ending in {{ㄹ}} drop it ({{살다|salda}} → {{사는|saneun}}, {{길다|gilda}} → {{긴|gin}}), and {{ㅂ}} verbs turn it into {{우|u}} ({{맵다|maepda}} → {{매운|maeun}}).

table: {{살다|salda}} → {{부산에 사는 친구|busane saneun chingu}} a friend who lives in Busan

blocks.p: **The subject inside takes {{이|i}}/{{가|ga}}.** Inside a describing part, the subject always takes {{이|i}}/{{가|ga}}, never {{은|eun}}/{{는|neun}}: {{키가 큰 사람|kiga keun saram}} “a tall person” (height-big person), {{제가 좋아하는 노래|jega joahaneun norae}} “the song I like”. {{은|eun}}/{{는|neun}} belongs to the whole sentence, not to the part that describes a noun.

blocks.p: **Done: {{-(으)ㄴ|-(eu)n}} on an action verb.** For something already done, action verbs take {{-ㄴ}} after a vowel and {{-은|-eun}} after a consonant: {{어제 본 영화|eoje bon yeonghwa}} “the movie I saw yesterday”, {{제가 만든 케이크|jega mandeun keikeu}} “the cake I made”, {{어제 먹은 음식|eoje meogeun eumsik}} “the food I ate yesterday”. On a descriptive verb, the same ending is the present ({{작은 방|jageun bang}}, lesson 40); on an action verb, it's the past. It's the {{-(으)ㄴ|-(eu)n}} of {{-(으)ㄴ 후에|-(eu)n hue}} and {{-(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요|-(eu)n jeogi isseoyo}}.

**Still to come: {{-(으)ㄹ|-(eu)l}}.** For something that hasn't happened yet: {{-ㄹ}} after a vowel, {{-을|-eul}} after a consonant. {{할 일|hal il}} “things to do”, {{먹을 거|meogeul geo}} “something to eat”, {{내일 만날 사람|naeil mannal saram}} “the person I'm meeting tomorrow”. blocks.p: **Doing, as a thing: {{-는 것|-neun geot}}.** An action verb with the modifier {{-는|-neun}} and {{것|geot}} “thing” turns an activity into a noun you can like, start, learn or talk about: {{요리하는 것|yorihaneun geot}} “cooking”, {{사진을 찍는 것|sajineul jjingneun geot}} “taking photos”. In speech {{것|geot}} is {{거|geo}}, and it melts with the particles:

**{{-기|-gi}} with a few describing verbs.** Stem + {{-기|-gi}} is another way to make “doing”, and it's the usual one before {{좋다|jota}}, {{싫다|silta}}, {{어렵다|eoryeopda}}, {{쉽다|swipda}}, {{힘들다|himdeulda}} and {{편하다|pyeonhada}}: {{이 동네는 살기 좋아요|i dongneneun salgi joayo}} “This neighborhood is a good place to live”, {{한국어는 배우기 어려워요?|hangugeoneun baeugi eoryeowoyo?}} “Is Korean hard to learn?”. You know this {{-기|-gi}} from {{-기 전에|-gi jeone}} and {{-기로 했어요|-giro haesseoyo}}.

blocks.p: **Soft opinions.** Koreans rarely state an opinion flatly. They add {{것 같아요|geot gatayo}} “it seems like”: {{비싸요|bissayo}} “it's expensive” → {{비싼 것 같아요|bissan geot gatayo}} “I think it's expensive”. It's for opinions, for guesses, and for sounding modest.
**Built on the modifiers.** {{것 같아요|geot gatayo}} comes after a modifier (lessons 40 and 41), so the modifier says the time:

table: {{비가 오는 것 같아요.|biga oneun geot gatayo.}} It seems to be raining.
{{좀 비싼 것 같아요.|jom bissan geot gatayo.}} I think it's a bit expensive.
{{민수 씨가 벌써 간 것 같아요.|minsu ssiga beolsseo gan geot gatayo.}} I think Minsu has already left.
{{비가 올 것 같아요.|biga ol geot gatayo.}} I think it'll rain.
{{저 사람은 학생인 것 같아요.|jeo sarameun haksaengin geot gatayo.}} I think that person is a student.

blocks.p: **My view, and a polite no.** {{제 생각에는|je saenggageneun}} “in my opinion” starts an opinion. And {{-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요|-(eu)l geot gatayo}} also softens a refusal: {{그날은 좀 힘들 것 같아요|geunareun jom himdeul geot gatayo}} “That day might be a bit difficult” is a kind way to say no. With feelings, it exaggerates: {{배고파서 죽을 것 같아요|baegopaseo jugeul geot gatayo}} “I'm starving (I feel I'll die).”

blocks.p: **Setting the scene: {{-는데|-neunde}}.** {{-는데|-neunde}} joins a background (what's going on, what you know) to the main point that follows: a question, a suggestion, a request or a surprise. English says it with “and”, “so”, “but”, or just a pause: {{배가 고픈데 뭐 먹을까요?|baega gopeunde mwo meogeulkkayo?}} “I'm hungry; shall we eat something?”, {{지금 마트에 가는데 뭐 필요해요?|jigeum mateue ganeunde mwo piryohaeyo?}} “I'm going to the supermarket: do you need anything?”

**The shape follows the modifiers.** Action verbs and {{있다|itda}}/{{없다|eopda}}: {{-는데|-neunde}} ({{가는데|ganeunde}}, {{없는데|eomneunde}}). Descriptive verbs: {{-(으)ㄴ데|-(eu)nde}} ({{고픈데|gopeunde}}, {{좋은데|joeunde}}). Nouns: {{인데|inde}} ({{학생인데|haksaenginde}}). Anything in the past: {{-았/었는데|-at/eonneunde}} ({{샀는데|sanneunde}}).

table: {{비가 오는데 우산 있어요?|biga oneunde usan isseoyo?}} It's raining; do you have an umbrella?
{{날씨가 좋은데 산책할까요?|nalssiga joeunde sanchaekalkkayo?}} It's nice out; shall we go for a walk?
{{저는 학생인데 할인돼요?|jeoneun haksaenginde harindwaeyo?}} I'm a student; can I get a discount?
{{어제 갔는데 문을 닫았어요.|eoje ganneunde muneul dadasseoyo.}} I went yesterday, but it was closed.

blocks.p: **A soft “but”.** Often the background contrasts with what follows: {{어제 갔는데 문을 닫았어요|eoje ganneunde muneul dadasseoyo}} “I went yesterday, but it was closed.” It's softer than {{-지만|-jiman}} and very common in speech. The {{그런데|geureonde}} and {{근데|geunde}} of lesson 34 are this same ending, between two sentences.

**Softening with {{-는데요|-neundeyo}}.** At the end of a sentence, {{-는데요|-neundeyo}} leaves it open so the other person can react: it sounds gentle, hesitant or polite. {{지금 회의 중인데요.|jigeum hoeui jungindeyo.}} “He's in a meeting right now…” (on the phone), {{저는 괜찮은데요.|jeoneun gwaenchaneundeyo.}} “I'm fine with it, though…”

blocks.p: **While doing, then: {{-다가|-daga}}.** Stem + {{-다가|-daga}} says you were in the middle of one thing when something else happened, or when you switched to something else: {{길을 걷다가 친구를 만났어요|gireul geotdaga chingureul mannasseoyo}} “I was walking down the street when I met a friend”, {{공부하다가 잠이 들었어요|gongbuhadaga jami deureosseoyo}} “I fell asleep while studying”. It has one shape for every stem, and the last verb carries the tense.

**Someone new, then someone known.** In a story, a person or thing that appears for the first time takes {{이|i}}/{{가|ga}}; once everyone knows who it is, it becomes the topic, with {{은|eun}}/{{는|neun}}. Korean folk tales begin exactly like this. It works like English “a man…” then “the man…”.

table: Once upon a time, there lived a tiger.

That person was a rice-cake seller.

blocks.p: **Story words.** {{처음에|cheoeume}} “at first”, {{그다음에|geudaeume}} “after that”, {{그때|geuttae}} “at that moment”, {{갑자기|gapjagi}} “suddenly”, {{그래서|geuraeseo}} “so”, {{그런데|geureonde}} “but then”, {{결국|gyeolguk}} “in the end”. And a background with {{-았/었는데|-at/eonneunde}} (lesson 44) sets up a surprise: {{집에 왔는데 아무도 없었어요|jibe wanneunde amudo eopseosseoyo}} “I got home, and nobody was there.”

blocks.means: telling what someone said without their exact words: “She said (that) she was tired.”

blocks.p: **Passing on what someone said.** Korean reports speech by putting the sentence into its plain form, then adding {{-고 했어요|-go haesseoyo}} “said that”. The plain form is the style of books and newspapers: {{-다|-da}}. Each kind of sentence has its own ending:

table: {{간다고 했어요|gandago haesseoyo}} said they're going; {{먹는다고 했어요|meongneundago haesseoyo}} said they eat it
{{바쁘다고 했어요|bappeudago haesseoyo}} said they're busy; {{있다고 했어요|itdago haesseoyo}}
{{학생이라고 했어요|haksaengirago haesseoyo}} said they're a student
{{올 거라고 했어요|ol georago haesseoyo}} said they'll come
{{시간 있냐고 했어요|sigan innyago haesseoyo}} asked if I had time
{{같이 가자고 했어요|gachi gajago haesseoyo}} suggested going together
{{기다리라고 했어요|gidarirago haesseoyo}} told me to wait

blocks.p: **Other verbs, and the short form.** Instead of {{했어요|haesseoyo}}, you can use {{말했어요|malhaesseoyo}} “said”, {{물어봤어요|mureobwasseoyo}} “asked” or {{들었어요|deureosseoyo}} “heard”: {{내일 눈이 온다고 들었어요|naeil nuni ondago deureosseoyo}} “I heard it's going to snow tomorrow.” The same ending gives your own thoughts: {{좋은 생각이라고 생각해요|joeun saenggagirago saenggakaeyo}} “I think it's a good idea.” In speech, {{-다고 해요|-dago haeyo}} shortens to {{-대요|-daeyo}}: {{바쁘대요|bappeudaeyo}} “She says she's busy.”

ex.tr: Mom told me to come over for dinner.
My friend suggested going on a trip together.
The teacher asked if I'd done my homework.
The news said it's going to snow tomorrow.
Jisu says she's busy these days.
I think Korean is fun.

blocks.tip: {{뭐라고요?|mworagoyo?}} “What did you say?” is the same {{-라고|-rago}}: a natural way to ask someone to repeat. Politer: {{네? 다시 한번 말씀해 주시겠어요?|ne? dasi hanbeon malsseumhae jusigesseoyo?}}

blocks.p: **Becoming: {{-아/어지다|-a/eojida}}.** A descriptive verb's present form without {{요|yo}}, plus {{지다|jida}}, means “to become, to get”: {{추워요|chuwoyo}} → {{추워지다|chuwojida}} “to get cold”, {{좋아요|joayo}} → {{좋아지다|joajida}} “to get better”. It then takes endings like any verb: {{추워졌어요|chuwojyeosseoyo}} “it's gotten cold”, {{좋아질 거예요|joajil geoyeyo}} “it'll get better”.

table: {{기분이 좋아졌어요.|gibuni joajyeosseoyo.}} I feel better now.
{{관광객이 많아졌어요.|gwangwanggaegi manajyeosseoyo.}} There are more tourists now.
{{더 예뻐졌네요!|deo yeppeojyeonneyo!}} You look even prettier!
{{이제 익숙해졌어요.|ije iksukaejyeosseoyo.}} I've gotten used to it now.

blocks.p: **Ending up: {{-게 되다|-ge doeda}}.** Stem + {{-게 되다|-ge doeda}} says something came about, often not by your own plan: {{한국에서 일하게 됐어요|hangugeseo ilhage dwaesseoyo}} “I ended up working in Korea”, {{그 사람을 좋아하게 됐어요|geu sarameul joahage dwaesseoyo}} “I came to like him”, {{알게 됐어요|alge dwaesseoyo}} “I found out”. It's also how Koreans share news modestly: {{다음 달에 결혼하게 됐어요|daeum dare gyeolhonhage dwaesseoyo}} “I'm getting married next month.” ({{됐어요|dwaesseoyo}} is the past of {{되다|doeda}}; {{돼서|dwaeseo}} is its {{-아서|-aseo}} form.)

ex.tr: The weather has gotten a lot warmer.
Prices have gone up a lot lately.
I started working out, and I've gotten healthier.

blocks.tip: {{늘다|neulda}} “to increase, to improve” is what Koreans say about a skill: {{한국어가 늘었어요|hangugeoga neureosseoyo}} “Your Korean has improved.” It's an {{ㄹ}} verb: {{늘었어요|neureosseoyo}}, {{느네요|neuneyo}}.

blocks.p: **I hope, I wish: {{-았/었으면 좋겠어요|-at/eosseumyeon jokesseoyo}}.** Word for word “if it happened, it would be good”: {{비가 그쳤으면 좋겠어요|biga geuchyeosseumyeon jokesseoyo}} “I wish the rain would stop.” The past shape ({{-았/었으면|-at/eosseumyeon}}) makes it sound like a wish; {{-(으)면 좋겠어요|-(eu)myeon jokesseoyo}} ({{비가 그치면 좋겠어요|biga geuchimyeon jokesseoyo}}) means the same and is just as common. Compare: to say what you want **to do**, {{-고 싶어요|-go sipeoyo}}; to hope something **happens**, {{-았/었으면 좋겠어요|-at/eosseumyeon jokesseoyo}}.

table: {{키가 좀 더 컸으면 좋겠어요.|kiga jom deo keosseumyeon jokesseoyo.}}
I wish I were a bit taller.
I hope you get well soon.

blocks.p: **Imagine: {{만약|manyak}} … {{-(으)면|-(eu)myeon}}.** {{만약|manyak}} “suppose, if” at the start makes a {{-(으)면|-(eu)myeon}} sentence clearly imaginary: {{만약 돈이 많으면 세계 여행을 할 거예요|manyak doni maneumyeon segye yeohaengeul hal geoyeyo}} “If I had lots of money, I'd travel around the world.” Korean needs no special “would”: {{-(으)ㄹ 거예요|-(eu)l geoyeyo}} does the job. And {{뭐 할 거예요?|mwo hal geoyeyo?}} asks “What would you do?”.

blocks.p: **You see: {{-거든요|-geodeunyo}}.** Stem + {{-거든요|-geodeunyo}} gives a reason or a background the listener didn't know, as an explanation: {{제가 요즘 바쁘거든요|jega yojeum bappeugeodeunyo}} “I'm busy these days, you see.” It often answers “why?”, or comes right after a request: {{좀 도와줄 수 있어요? 제가 한국어를 잘 못하거든요.|jom dowajul su isseoyo? jega hangugeoreul jal motageodeunyo.}} “Could you help me? My Korean isn't very good, you see.” Past: {{-았/었거든요|-at/eotgeodeunyo}}; after a noun, {{(이)거든요|(i)geodeunyo}}.

**You know: {{-잖아요|-janayo}}.** Stem + {{-잖아요|-janayo}} reminds the listener of something they already know, or should: {{제가 고기를 안 먹잖아요|jega gogireul an meokjanayo}} “I don't eat meat, remember?”, {{오늘 금요일이잖아요|oneul geumyoirijanayo}} “It's Friday, you know.” Said with a smile, it's friendly; with a sharp tone, it means “Obviously!”.

table: {{내일 시험이 있거든요.|naeil siheomi itgeodeunyo.}} I have a test tomorrow, you see.
{{내일 시험이 있잖아요.|naeil siheomi itjanayo.}} We have a test tomorrow, remember?

blocks.p: **Where to use them.** Both belong to conversation, and you'll hear them constantly in dramas; both are polite with {{요|yo}}. In writing or a formal talk, use {{-아서|-aseo}} or {{-(으)니까|-(eu)nikka}} instead.

ex.tr: Sorry I'm late. The traffic was terrible, you see.

ex.t: 이거 제가 만들었어요. 요리하는 걸 좋아하거든요.
ex.tr: I made this. I love cooking, you see.
ex.r: igeo jega mandeureosseoyo. yorihaneun geol joahageodeunyo.

ex.t: 저는 저녁에 커피를 못 마셔요. 잠을 못 자거든요.
ex.tr: I can't drink coffee in the evening. I can't sleep, you see.
ex.r: jeoneun jeonyeoge keopireul mot masyeoyo. jameul mot jageodeunyo.

ex.tr: You know I can't eat spicy food!
It's Friday, you know. Let's have a drink!

blocks.tip: {{있잖아요|itjanayo}} on its own, at the start, is a way to get someone's attention before you tell them something: “You know what?”

lessons.title: Talk to friends
lessons.summary: Switch to casual speech with close friends: “What are you doing?”, “Wanna eat?”, “Let's go!”, and know when not to.
lessons.topic: {{반말|banmal}}, casual speech: dropping {{요|yo}}; {{이야|iya}}/{{야|ya}}; {{나|na}}, {{너|neo}}, {{내|nae}}, {{네|ne}}; {{응|eung}}/{{아니|ani}}; {{-자|-ja}} “let's”; {{-(으)ㄹ래?|-(eu)llae?}} “wanna?”

blocks.p: **Casual speech.** With close friends, younger siblings, and younger people once you're close, Koreans drop the polite endings: this is {{반말|banmal}}, “half speech”. Mostly, you simply drop {{요|yo}}: {{뭐 해요?|mwo haeyo?}} → {{뭐 해?|mwo hae?}}, {{좋아요|joayo}} → {{좋아|joa}}, {{갔어요|gasseoyo}} → {{갔어|gasseo}}, {{갈게요|galgeyo}} → {{갈게|galge}}.

**What else changes.** {{이에요|ieyo}}/{{예요|yeyo}} become {{이야|iya}}/{{야|ya}}. {{저|jeo}} “I” becomes {{나|na}} (and {{제가|jega}} → {{내가|naega}}), {{제|je}} “my” becomes {{내|nae}}, and “you” is {{너|neo}} ({{네|ne}} “your”, often said {{니|ni}} so it doesn't sound like {{내|nae}}). To call a friend: the name + {{아|a}} after a consonant, {{야|ya}} after a vowel: {{민준아!|minjuna!}}, {{수지야!|sujiya!}}

**Let's, and wanna?** {{-자|-ja}} is the casual “let's”: {{가자!|gaja!}} “let's go!”, {{먹자|meokja}} “let's eat”. {{-(으)ㄹ래?|-(eu)llae?}} asks what someone feels like doing: {{먹을래?|meogeullae?}} “wanna eat?”, {{갈래?|gallae?}} “wanna go?”. Answer {{응, 좋아|eung, joa}} or {{아니, 괜찮아|ani, gwaenchana}}. The casual “please do” is just the present form without {{요|yo}}: {{빨리 와!|ppalli wa!}} “come quick!”

**When to switch.** Don't start in {{반말|banmal}}: it's for people who have agreed to it. An older or same-age friend may say {{우리 말 놓을까요?|uri mal noeulkkayo?}} “Shall we drop the formalities?”. Until then, keep {{요|yo}}; with strangers, older people and at work, always.

ex.tr: I'm starving right now.
Are you free tomorrow?
Let's watch a movie!
Wanna get a coffee?
Okay, got it.
Suji, is this yours?

blocks.tip: {{어디서|eodiseo}} is the everyday short form of {{어디에서|eodieseo}}, in polite speech too. And {{이따 봐!|itta bwa!}} “see you later!” is {{이따가 봐요|ittaga bwayo}} without {{요|yo}}.

mistakes.why: {{반말|banmal}} is only for close friends and younger people who've agreed to it; to your boss, the honorific.
Casual speech has no {{요|yo}}: {{학생이야|haksaengiya}}.
After a consonant, call a friend with {{아|a}}: {{민준아|minjuna}}. After a vowel, {{야|ya}}: {{수지야|sujiya}}.
